turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, the big question for you is, it feels like it's really working, and this is very difficult to do at a company of that scale. A lot of leaders are trying to make it work. What are two or three things that you've done that you think have been most impactful and effective in helping Cisco lean into AI, not be scared of it, and actually embrace the future?
turns.zh: 所以，对你们来说，关键问题在于：这一切似乎确实奏效，而在如此大规模的企业中做到这点实属不易。许多领导者都在努力实现这一目标。在帮助思科拥抱AI、克服恐惧、迎接未来方面，哪些措施最具影响力和成效？

turns.speaker: Jeetu Patel
turns.en: Innovation in my mind is a choice. I always find it interesting when people say, "Well, you're a large company, you can innovate. You're a small company, you can innovate." It's like, "No, it's just a choice. Every day you come into work and you can choose to be thinking about being creative, or you can choose to not be creative." It's like a little binary ... It's a binary choice You can make every hour, every minute of every day. And so, we made that choice that says, Cisco is going to be not just an iconic company. And Chuck Robbins, our CEO says this very eloquently. He's like, "I want Cisco not just to be an iconic company. I want Cisco to also be an iconic and innovative company." And so, we got to make sure that we are actually innovating with the set of constraints that we are dealt with. (00:10:30): Every company has their own set of constraints, and we have our own set of constraints, and we have to make sure that given those constraints, we have to actually innovate really well. Now, what are the two or three things that have happened that have really helped us out? One was, being very clear on what is up for debate and what is not up for debate. Because what can end up happening is you can always have a pocket veto in a large company where if you ask enough number of people, people say no. If you're a large company, you ask enough number of people, someone's going to say no, right? And so, when you have conviction about something that's happening, that is going to be a bet that you need to place. (00:11:10): What most people think in large companies is large companies don't experiment. That is in fact not true. Large companies experiment a lot. What large companies don't do is when an experiment works, they don't go all in and double down. They try to keep hedging. We didn't hedge on AI. We said we were going to go all in. That was number one. (00:11:31): What that meant was we had to get people to understand that their personal success and the success of the company are very aligned in us getting dexterous with the use of AI. That means that if they feel like for some reason AI is going to take their job or AI is going to be negative for them, we had to reassure them that that was not the case. But the reverse was guaranteed to be the case, that if you didn't choose AI, if you weren't going to be dexterous in whatever job function you're doing, then your job is probably not going to be that relevant over here in the long run. (00:12:08): So, that was the first thing that we did, that was a, I'm not a big fan of top-down hierarchy of going out and doing things. In fact, deep down inside I don't respect hierarchy as much. I feel like it can constrain you at times. But I wanted to make ... On this one we were very, very deliberate. The entire company is on the same page, we are an AI-first company. And this happened, we were working towards it even prior to ChatGPT, but ChatGPT became that seminal moment in November of '22 that we actually did that. So, that was one. (00:12:42): Number two was we had to make sure that we defined what success looked like. The way that individual success was defined was everyone wanted to be a GM at Cisco. They wanted to own their own fiefdom, be a general manager. Because they felt like, "In order for me to move up the ranks, I need to be a general manager, which means I need to have my own sales team. I need to have my own marketing team. I need to have my own product team. I need to have my own engineering team. I'm going to make sure I run my own silo." And if you're a 40 billion business in product revenues, 45 billion whatever we were at the time, and then all of a sudden your goal is that you're going to just run a bunch of $40 million businesses and break it up into a series of 40 million businesses, that's actually not a good thing for the company. (00:13:30): So, the thing we did was we said, "We have to become not a holding company of 251 acquisitions and thousands of different products, we have to become a platform company." And the characteristic of the platform is you have to be tightly integrated where the customer feels the same emotion, no matter what product of ours they use. There's the same set of expectations that can be served, reliability, trust, elegance and design, solving a problem in the most efficient way. Those are the things we want to strive to do. But you don't have to buy everything all at once, because we also want to be realistic about the fact that not every customer only uses Cisco top to bottom. There's an ecosystem. So, loosely coupled, but tightly integrated. You don't have to buy everything all at once, but boy, when you do buy two things together, they work like magic. So, that was the second big thing we did. (00:14:22): And then the third one we did was we said, "Let's make sure that we have a mental model shift in the company." And we did this about five, five and a half years ago when I first joined. This was a very deliberate decision, which was, we cannot operate in a walled garden. We have to make sure that we operate in an open ecosystem, which means we have to be completely comfortable with having a competitor that we're going to partner with. And that's okay. We don't have to think about this in a zero-sum manner. In order for me to win, someone has to lose. (00:14:58): We can partner, because if a customer has made a choice of going with company A and company B and we happen to be one of those two companies, we owe it to the customer to invest in their success in that other company because if the customer succeeds, that success has a flow through rate to you that's going to be pretty high. And so, that's what we did, and I think that's been those principles of building great products, but making sure that it operates like a platform and having an open ecosystem, I think has been kind of central. And then not being confused about the fact that we'll be AI-first from the top down.
turns.zh:
对我来说，创新是一种选择。每当听到人们说"你们是大公司，所以能创新；你们是小公司，所以能创新"时，我总觉得很有趣。这就像在说，"不，这只是一种选择。每天上班时，你可以选择发挥创造力，也可以选择不去创新。"这就像一个二元选择……每小时、每分钟你都能做出这样的选择。因此，我们做出了这样的选择：思科不仅要成为一家标志性公司。我们的首席执行官查克·罗宾斯曾雄辩地说："我希望思科不仅是标志性公司，还要成为创新型标志性公司。" 因此，我们必须确保在现有约束条件下真正创新。（00:10:30）：每家公司都有自己的约束条件，我们也不例外。在这些约束条件下，我们必须确保能够出色地创新。那么，有哪些两三件事对我们帮助巨大呢？首先，明确哪些可以讨论，哪些不可以讨论至关重要。因为在大公司里，总会有人用否决权阻止创新。例如，如果你询问足够多的人，总会有人反对。如果是大公司，肯定会有人否决某项提议，对吧？因此，当你对某项决策深信不疑时，你就必须下注。这就是信念的力量。（00:11:10）：大多数人认为大公司不爱尝试新事物，这其实并不正确。大公司经常进行实验，但当实验成功后，却不愿全力以赴地推进创新，总是犹豫不决。我们在AI领域没有犹豫，坚定选择全力投入。这是首要任务。（00:11:31）：这意味着我们必须让员工明白，个人成功与公司成功紧密相连——掌握AI技术至关重要。这意味着，如果员工出于某种原因认为AI会取代他们的工作，或者对他们不利，我们必须安抚他们的顾虑。但反之亦然：如果你不选择AI，如果你不善于利用AI技术来提升自己的工作能力，那么你的职位在未来很可能变得无关紧要。（00:12:08）：因此，这是我们首先要做的。我不喜欢自上而下的强制推行模式。事实上，内心深处我对等级制度并不敬重，觉得它有时会束缚人手。但在这一点上，我们格外谨慎。全公司上下达成共识：我们要成为以AI为先的公司。早在ChatGPT出现之前，我们就朝着这个目标努力，但2022年11月ChatGPT的问世让这一愿景成为现实。（00:12:42）：第二点是，我们必须明确成功的定义。个人成功的定义是：每个人都想成为思科的总经理。他们希望拥有自己的势力范围，成为总经理。因为他们认为："要晋升到更高层级，我就必须成为总经理，这意味着我需要拥有自己的销售团队、市场团队、产品团队和工程团队。我要确保自己能独立运营自己的部门。"而如果是一家市值400亿美元的公司……
在产品收入方面，当时我们的营收规模约为45亿美元。突然间，你的目标变成了只经营一堆价值4000万美元的业务，并将其拆分成一系列价值4000万美元的独立项目，但这对公司来说其实并非良策。（00:13:30）因此，我们决定："我们不能再做一家拥有251项收购、数千种不同产品的控股公司，而必须转型为平台型公司。"平台型公司的核心特征是高度整合——无论客户使用我们的哪款产品，都能感受到一致的体验。所有产品都需满足同一套标准：可靠性、信任、优雅设计，以及以最高效的方式解决问题。这些都是我们致力于达成的目标。不过无需一次性整合所有产品，因为我们也要面对现实——并非每个客户都会全程使用思科产品。生态系统才是关键。因此，平台应保持松散耦合与紧密整合的平衡。无需一次性整合所有产品，但当两款产品协同使用时，效果往往惊喜连连。这就是我们实施的第二项重大改革。

（00:14:22）第三项改革是确立"公司思维模式转变"。大约五年半前我加入公司时便开始推动这一变革。这是一个深思熟虑的决策：我们不能固守封闭式生态，必须拥抱开放式生态。这意味着我们要坦然接受与竞争对手合作共赢的局面，不必以零和思维看待竞争。（00:14:58）合作共赢的核心逻辑是：若客户选择A公司和B公司，而我们恰好是其中之一，我们有责任助力客户在另一家公司的成功。客户的成功将反哺我们自身。因此，我们始终秉持"以平台思维打造卓越产品"和"构建开放生态"的核心原则。同时，我们始终清醒认识到，公司自上而下将以AI为核心驱动力，实现创新引领。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to take a tangent and make sure people understand what Cisco even does these days. I think as a lay person, you'll think about Cisco and you're like, "Okay, they WebEx, yes. They make maybe some routers." You guys are key to this massive AI infrastructure build-out that's happening right now. You're a major player in this. I don't think people realize this, people listening to this podcast. Give us just a quick glimpse into how Cisco fits into this massive build-out and just what does Cisco these days?
turns.zh: 我想稍微偏题一下，确保大家能理解思科如今到底在做些什么。我觉得作为外行，你可能会认为思科就是做WebEx的，对吧，或许还生产些路由器。但实际上，如今你们在推动这场大规模的AI基础设施建设中发挥着关键作用。你们是其中的重要参与者。我觉得听这个播客的人可能没有意识到这一点。所以能否请您简要讲讲思科如何融入这场大规模的建设中，以及思科如今的业务重点是什么？

turns.speaker: Jeetu Patel
turns.en: Cisco is a critical infrastructure company for the AI era. What does that mean? But if you think about where the constraints are right now, if you think that AI is going to be one of the biggest movements, and then you ask yourself the question, "What could hold AI back?" There's three things where we feel like we can have a direct impact that can hold AI back. Number one is there's an infrastructure constraint. There's just not enough power compute and network bandwidth in the world to go out and satiate the needs of AI. (00:16:31): Number two is, there's a trust deficit. If people don't trust these systems, they're not going to use them. And right now there's a lot of mistrust in these systems. Hallucination is a feature when you're writing poetry, but when you're trying to go out and run predictable systems, hallucination can be a bad thing. And these models are unpredictable, they're non-deterministic, and so they have to make sure that they have safety and security factored into them. (00:16:56): And then the third area is a data gap. So far we've trained these models with human-generated data publicly available on the internet, but we are running out of human-generated data publicly available on the internet to train the models. And every company is going to differentiate based on their own proprietary enterprise data being used to train the models, synthetic data and machine data, which is where the most amount of growth is. And the third category of machine data we can play a massive role in at Cisco. So, what does Cisco do then? If you think about a GPU, which is what everyone now is very clear because of the great job that Jensen has done that here's what a GPU's core contribution is to AI. If these GPUs aren't networked together, you don't have AI, because it used to be that you could train a model on a single GPU, but then what happened was the model got too big to be put on a single GPU. So then you had a server with eight GPUs that got connected together. So, you could train a model with eight GPUs. (00:17:58): But then that wasn't good enough. So, then what happened was you said, "I'm going to have a rack of servers that I'm going to network together." That at some point wasn't big enough. And so then they said, "I'm going to have a cluster of racks that are connected together." And that connected together is the operative word. That's what we end up doing is NVIDIA makes the GPUs and we connect those GPUs together. AMD makes the GPUs, we connect them together. (00:18:24): And now what's happened, Lenny, is you have these data centers that might be hundreds of kilometers apart that need to operate like one coherent cluster, which means that they're completely in sync. Every GPU is in sync with each other when you're doing a training run. And that requires a very sophisticated set of technologies that we build to make sure that you could have two data centers, 800 kilometers apart, but boy, they run completely in sync with each other. And that's what Cisco does. We provide the networking, we provide the optics technology, we provide the safety and security technology, we provide the observability, we provide the data platform, all of those things together for making sure that we provide critical infrastructure for the AI era.
turns.zh:
思科是人工智能时代的关键基础设施公司。这意味着什么？但如果你思考当前面临的制约因素，如果你认为人工智能将成为最重大的变革之一，然后问自己"是什么在阻碍人工智能的发展？"我们认为有三个方面可以产生直接影响。首先是基础设施瓶颈。当前全球的算力和网络带宽根本不足以满足人工智能的需求。（00:16:31）  
其次是信任缺失。如果人们不信任这些系统，就不会使用它们。目前公众对这些系统存在诸多不信任。幻觉在诗歌创作中是特色，但在运行可预测系统时，幻觉可能带来负面影响。这些模型不可预测、非确定性，因此必须确保其安全性和可靠性。（00:16:56）  
第三是数据鸿沟。迄今为止，我们使用互联网公开数据训练模型，但这些数据即将枯竭。每家公司都将基于自身专有企业数据（用于训练模型）、合成数据和机器数据进行差异化竞争，而后者将成为增长的主要动力。思科在机器数据领域可以发挥重要作用。  
那么思科具体做了什么？以GPU为例，由于Jensen的出色工作，人们对GPU在人工智能中的核心贡献已有清晰认识。但如果GPU无法互联，就无法实现人工智能。过去可以用单个GPU训练模型，但随着模型规模不断扩大，单个GPU无法承载。因此，人们开始将8个GPU连接到服务器上。然而这仍不够，于是又将多个服务器机架互联。如今，数据中心可能相隔数百公里，但需要像单个集群般无缝协作。这意味着在训练过程中，所有GPU必须完全同步。这就需要我们构建复杂的技术体系，确保相隔800公里的两个数据中心能实现完全同步。思科正是通过提供网络、光学技术、安全防护、可观测性及数据平台，构建起人工智能时代的关键基础设施。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, being on the inside of this massive investment that is happening across the world, what do you think isn't being priced in into where things are heading into how much life will change, or just the scale of this build out?
turns.zh: 既然身处这场全球大规模投资的核心，你认为哪些因素尚未被市场定价？比如事态的发展方向、生活将发生多大程度的变革，或者说这场建设的规模究竟有多大？

turns.speaker: Jeetu Patel
turns.en: Years ago I'd had a chance to meet with Ray Kurzweil. He's the chief scientist at Google for a while, and I think he still is. And he had talked about, he was writing this book called Live Long Enough to Live Forever. And so I was talking to him, I'm like, "What is the impact to human population if all of a sudden you can have 15 generations living simultaneously, because we have an indefinite span of life? Because now all of a sudden everything has to change. How does housing work, housing work? How does agriculture work? How does transportation work? How does ... Everything changes?" And he looked at me and he had the most profound answer and he said, "Most people can't think exponentially, because they always think exponentially maybe on a single dimension." But what ends up happening in these things is you can sometimes you have to keep in mind that exponentiality happens across multiple dimensions all at once. (00:20:21): So, if you do have an indefinite span of life, you have to assume that humans are creative enough that they're going to find a way to have a three-day crop cycle. And they probably will have 5,000 story skyscrapers, and there will be a bunch of things in society that we have assumed are not solvable that'll now be solvable. (00:20:44): So, when you go back to your question and say, what changes in this entire equation that has not been factored in well? I think today AI is looked at largely as a productivity tool and an aggregation mechanism. I have data all over and I'm going to be able to make sure that language can be used to compose the data in a way that I can give you, Lenny, the answer to the question that you're looking for that I think is the 0.0001% of the tip of the iceberg. (00:21:17): The reality is, is we will have original insights generated that don't exist in the human corpus of knowledge, and we will have the physical world get augmented to language where capacity is augmented to humans. And what we have to be careful of is that that capacity is working on behalf of humans, but if that capacity is augmented to humans, you can now do things that you really care to do, and not do things that you don't care to do. And so our biggest realization that we had when we were using Codex, for example, when we were writing a code with OpenAI's kind of model and development tool, was the first three months we were screwing around with this. And then there was this light bulb that runoffs. In fact, there was a former deployed engineer from OpenAI that told us about this, which is, "Hey, stop trying to think of this as a tool. Think of this as a teammate that got added to your team, and your framing will change, and the way in which you actually use the technology will change." (00:22:33): And that essentially, if you compound that to how society operates, that's going to be pretty profound as an implication, while keeping in mind that these safety and security risks are non-trivial and they're real. And you can't be completely flippant about them, because how an AI identifies its own success and its own ambition will really matter. And we have to make sure that we actually keep guardrails around that, because it is in service of humans, it is not to go out and build a society by itself. And I do think that those are important kind of checks and balances you have to keep in mind. (00:23:17): But the thing that people sometimes miss out in this very polarized narrative, which is we are either going to have nothing to do in society, or this is going to be completely useless as a piece of technology. I think that's not a helpful narrative. In fact, what is helpful is saying, "As we reconstruct society for the next phase, how can we make sure that life gets infinitely better? How can we make sure that diseases get solved? How can we make sure that poverty gets eradicated? How can we make sure that how people learn and find excitement and joy out of life gets compounded meaningfully?" If that happens, I think there's goodness that comes out of this.
turns.zh:
多年前，我曾有机会与雷·库兹韦尔（Ray Kurzweil）见面。他曾是谷歌的首席科学家，现在想必仍在此职位上。当时他谈到自己正在撰写一本名为《活得足够久，直到永生》的书。我问他："如果人类寿命无限延长，一下子能有15代人同时生活，这对人类社会会有什么影响？因为现在一切都必须改变。住房如何运作？农业如何运作？交通如何运作？所有事物都会发生巨变！"他看着我，给出了最深刻的回答："大多数人无法进行指数级思考，因为他们往往只在单一维度上考虑指数级问题。"但现实中指数级增长可能同时发生在多个维度上。（00:20:21）所以，如果人类寿命无限延长，我们必须假设人类足够有创造力，能找到实现三天作物生长周期的方法。人类很可能建造5000层的摩天大楼，社会中许多我们认为无法解决的问题将迎刃而解。（00:20:44）回到你的问题：整个方程式中还有哪些关键因素尚未被充分考虑？如今人工智能主要被视为生产力工具和信息聚合机制。我拥有大量数据，能用语言组织这些数据，给你，莱尼，你所寻求的答案或许只是冰山一角。（00:21:17）现实情况是，我们将产生人类知识库中不存在的原创见解，物理世界将被赋予语言能力，从而提升人类的认知能力。我们必须警惕这种能力是为人类服务的，但如果能力被过度增强，人就能专注于自己真正关心的任务，而避免做那些不愿做的事。例如，在使用Codex时，我们最初三个月都在摸索，后来突然灵光一现。OpenAI的前工程师告诉我们："别把它当作工具，而是当作加入团队的队友，这样你的思维方式和技术应用方式都会发生转变。"（00:22:33）从本质上讲，如果将其应用于社会运作，影响将是深远的，但我们必须时刻警惕安全风险，这些风险绝非无关紧要。我们不能对此掉以轻心，因为AI如何界定自身成功与野心，至关重要。我们必须确保建立必要的监管机制，因为AI服务于人类，而不是自行构建社会。这是我们必须牢记的重要制衡机制。（00:23:17）但人们有时会忽视这种极端化的叙事：要么认为人工智能让社会闲置，要么认为它作为技术毫无用处。我认为
这种说法并无益处。实际上，真正有益的应该是这样问："在为下一阶段重建社会的过程中，我们如何确保生活能不断改善？我们如何确保疾病得以治愈？我们如何确保贫困被消除？我们如何确保人们学习知识、从生活中获得激情与快乐的能力能得到显著提升？"如果能做到这些，我相信这场危机终将带来积极的成果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A line that I often think about is, Huang has had this thought that the best case scenario with AI, because he was a very AI doomer for a long time, and I think the reason he got leaned into AI is like, "I need to help steer this in a direction that isn't going to harm the world." The way he described it is, "The best case scenario for humanity is we're the house cat, where AI is just like, 'Okay, nice. Just keep sitting here with me and I'll take care of you.'"
turns.zh: 有一句话我常回想起来：黄仁勋曾说过，关于AI的最乐观情景是——毕竟他长期对AI持悲观态度——而他投身AI领域的初衷是，“我需要帮助引导AI的发展方向，确保它不会危害人类。”他形容道：“对人类而言，最理想的未来是我们成为‘家猫’，而AI只是‘好的，不错。继续坐在这里陪我，我会照顾好你的。’”

turns.speaker: Jeetu Patel
turns.en: But by the way, the things that he is doing right now are nothing short of extraordinary. And for all the critique that one can have, the level of deep thinking that's going on with his company, it's just crazy.
turns.zh: 不过说真的，他目前所做的一切都堪称非凡。无论外界如何批评，他的公司所进行的深度思考，其深度和广度都令人惊叹。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, as you've been thinking about where things are heading, I've been liking to ask this question with people with kids, is there anything you're kind of shifting in how you raise your daughter, keeping in mind where things are heading? Are there skills you're trying to instill in her values you're trying to instill in her that will help her thrive in this future?
turns.zh: 所以，当你思考未来走向时，我想问问那些有孩子的朋友们：考虑到未来的发展，你们在养育女儿时是否有任何转变？是否有特定的技能或价值观在努力灌输给她，以帮助她在未来蓬勃发展？

turns.speaker: Jeetu Patel
turns.en: We made a choice, and I didn't know how that choice was going to go. That was actually not even an active choice, it was a passive choice. Frankly, even might have been slightly intellectually lazy in the way that we did it, but it actually worked out pretty well in the sense that we didn't really deprive her of the use of technology. There's a school of thought that says, "Keep technology away from the kids for a while." We didn't do that. And frankly, I didn't know how it was going to work out, because there are things about the way that the generation is, and by the way, all of us, not just new generation, but this kind of constantly being glued to your phone all the time and not being able to actually put that down and have a conversation. I think it's an important skill in humans to have and preserve over time. (00:25:45): And in fact, as AI does more for us, we should be able to have more of this time. I don't have to worry about every notification that's coming on my phone every minute of the day, because maybe I can be more present in the moment that I'm in. She just turned 15 and the night before she was turning 15, what I realized is she is so emotionally mature. We were sitting down one night and she's like, "Hey dad, just so you know, I feel really good right now about having a very strong value system." I'm like, "Oh, okay, what does that mean? And say more." And she's like, "Well, can you name five things that you feel so convicted about that if the entire world disagreed with you," this is the day before she's turning 15, okay? "The entire world disagreed with you. You would still feel like you were right on that and that would waver you." She's like, "I have a certain core set of things that I believe in where I am completely confident that if everyone disagreed with me, I'm still good." (00:26:56): Now, by the way, I have to kind of coach her on the, "Hey, when you get new data, be open-minded to changing your mind." But it was actually a very interesting dynamic, which is, if we can have them be exposed to technology but have the right value system, you might actually have the best of both worlds. And the day ain't over yet. She's 15. There's a lot of chances for her getting influenced by external factors and all of that. But what you have to do is make sure that you instill the right values, but then also expose them to the reality of what the world is today and not completely insulate them from that. (00:27:33): And so, the way that it worked out, it did end up working well, and we were lucky for no credit to us she was able to use technology to get her EQ higher and higher, and we were lucky on that front. And we know it can go sideways the other way too. But I do feel like right now, at least for my one daughter, what we try to do is get her exposed to the technology, but make sure that we focus a lot more on the values that we need to have that govern us on a day-to-day basis. Kindness, not being arrogant, hard work, work ethic, those things matter. And those are timeless in my mind. I don't think those change, because take risks, be creative, that kind of stuff.
turns.zh: 我们做了一个选择，但我当时并不知道这个选择会如何发展。实际上这甚至不是一个主动的选择，而是一个被动的选择。说实话，我们做这件事的方式可能有些不够用心，但结果还不错，因为我们并没有剥夺她使用科技的权利。有些人主张“让孩子们暂时远离科技”。我们没有这么做。说实话，我当时也不知道结果会怎样，因为这一代人的成长方式，以及我们所有人——不只是新一代人——总是不停地盯着手机，无法放下手机进行交流。我认为这是一项人类必须长期保持的重要技能。（00:25:45）事实上，随着人工智能为我们做更多事情，我们应该能有更多这样的时间。我不必担心手机上每分钟弹出的每条通知，因为这样我就能更专注于当下所处的时刻。她刚满15岁，前一晚她即将迎来15岁生日时，我意识到她在情感上已经非常成熟。有一天晚上，她说：“爸爸，你知道吗，我现在对拥有一套强大的价值观感觉特别好。”我说：“哦，好，什么意思？再说说。”她说：“嗯，你能不能列出五件你坚信不疑的事情，就算全世界都反对你，你也会坚持自己的观点。” 这是在她即将满15岁的前一晚，好吗？“全世界都反对你，你仍然会坚信自己是对的。”她说：“我有一套自己深信不疑的核心价值观，就算全世界都反对我，我也依然坚信自己是正确的。” （00:26:56）说真的，我得提醒她：“嘿，当你获得新信息时，要保持开放心态，愿意改变自己的想法。” 但这其实是一个非常有趣的动态——如果我们能让他们接触科技，同时拥有正确的价值观，或许就能两全其美。今天还没结束呢。她15岁了。她还有很多机会受到外界因素的影响等等。但你必须确保灌输正确的价值观，同时也要让她接触当今世界的现实，不能完全与世隔绝。（00:27:33）所以，最终结果确实不错。我们很幸运——不是因为我们功劳大——她能够利用科技不断提升自己的情商，在这方面我们很幸运。我们知道情况也可能朝着相反方向发展。但我确实觉得现在，至少对我的一个女儿来说，我们努力做的是让她接触科技，但同时更注重日常生活中必须遵循的价值观。善良、不傲慢、勤奋、职业道德，这些都很重要。在我看来，它们是永恒的。我不认为这些会改变，因为要冒险、要有创造力之类的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Jeetu, these are parenting goals. As I hear this, I have a two and a half year old Ms, it sounds like you've done an amazing job raising your daughter.
turns.zh: 吉图，这些都是为人父母的目标。听你这么说，我有两个半岁的女儿，感觉你把女儿养得太棒了。

turns.speaker: Jeetu Patel
turns.en: I would take zero credit for it. I think she deserves a lot of credit for growing up to be who she's become. And her mother.
turns.zh: 我一点功劳都不敢领。我觉得她成长为今天的样子，完全值得赞赏。还有她的母亲。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got to shout out mom. What's interesting is that I know Anthropic is really big, this idea of values and just how you operate. Anthropic has this constitution they released of how the values essentially of Claude. And it's so interesting how much similarity there is to how to raise a great person and to how to steer an AI correctly.
turns.zh: 得向妈妈大声致谢。有趣的是，我知道Anthropic公司非常重视价值观，以及企业运营方式。他们发布了一份宪章，详细阐述了Claude的核心价值观。令人惊讶的是，在培养优秀人才和正确引导人工智能这两件事上，竟有诸多相通之处。

turns.speaker: Jeetu Patel
turns.en: That's right. And by the way, some of your beliefs and your system around you might change, but values tend to be pretty long lasting. And culture and a company tends to be pretty long lasting. Ben Horowitz talks about this very eloquently. The culture is just a set of norms that accompany action. It's not a set of beliefs, it's a set of behaviors that you exude within the company. And it's actually very, very true, because when things aren't going right, how do people behave to go solve problems and come together? And that actually forms your cultural norms. And I think those cultural norms, it's very important to be intentional about it. And as you have more automation in the world, being intentional not just with humans but also with machines and what you want to do to create the guardrails, I think is pretty important.
turns.zh: 没错。顺便说一句，你周围的一些信念和体系可能会变，但价值观往往经久不衰。企业文化也同样能经受住时间考验。本·霍洛维茨对此阐述得非常精彩。企业文化不过是一套伴随行动的规范体系。它不是一套信仰，而是公司内部流露的行为准则。这确实千真万确。当事情进展不顺时，人们如何行动来解决问题、团结协作？这些行为最终形成了文化规范。我认为有意识地塑造这种文化规范至关重要。随着世界自动化程度加深，不仅要关注人类，更要关注机器，建立必要的约束机制，这一点尤为重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm going to take us in a different direction. I talked to Aaron Levie, your former boss at Box.
turns.zh: 接下来我们转换话题。我采访了Aaron Levie，他曾是Box公司的上司。

turns.speaker: Jeetu Patel
turns.en: Dear, dear friend.
turns.zh: 亲爱的朋友。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And friend. I asked him just what should I ask you about with something that he learned from you that has stuck with him ever since working with you? And he share this concept of the right to win, which he says has informed the way he thinks about strategy ever since. Talk about what this is and how folks might use this when they're thinking about product strategy, company strategy?
turns.zh: 朋友啊。我问他，有没有从你这里学到、至今仍影响着他战略思考的理念？他提到了“赢得胜利的权利”这个概念，称自从与你共事后，这一理念始终指导着他的战略思维。能否解释一下这个概念，以及人们在思考产品战略、公司战略时如何运用它？

turns.speaker: Jeetu Patel
turns.en: One of the things that we would always talk about is in the areas that we are going to participate, do we have permission to play? Every company has to make sure that the way in which they provide points of insertion and logical entry into a market is a lot of times dependent on, do you have the permission to play in that market? Do you have an avenue to have a route to market to be able to take that product? Just by building a product that is amazing in some area, you don't end up actually getting it to mass scale distribution. And so, one of the things that we would always do is ask ourselves a question. "We're building this new category or we're building this new capability. Is it going to be logical for people that Box built it versus another company building it? Is it going to be logical for people that Cisco built it versus another company building it?" (00:31:18): So, that's this notion of permission to play, the right to win. Do we have a right to win in that area because we have permission to play? And do we have the route to market to be able to take that product and get it to mass scale distribution? And if you can do those things right, then actually your dollars that you expend on building product actually have an outsized return. If not, then you can actually end up spending a lot of money on product. Where the product people think, "Ah, these sales guys don't get it. They don't know how to sell it, especially in enterprise software." And sales people think, "These product guys don't get it. They don't know how to build it." (00:31:56): And so, I think in order to stop that, what you have to do is you have to actually use your scale as an advantage and you have to use the areas where you've got the ability to have permission to play where people feel like this is very logical for a company like Cisco. When we say we are going to network the GPUs and make sure that we actually have a trusted system in AI, that is not far-fetched for someone to go out and think about, because it's a very natural thing for us to do, because for the past 40 years we've been doing it for the rest of the infrastructure that was not AI. And so, that's not a far cry to say, "Okay, we'll now do it for AI." (00:32:35): And I think that was an area that Aaron and I spent a fair ... And by the way, I'm glad that he took that out of me. There's so much I've learned from him. The biggest area I've learned from him is, you never give up. And persistence beats intellect, and stamina beats intellect any day of the week, twice on Sunday. And that guy is as smart as they come, but that's not the biggest reason he's successful. The biggest reason he's successful is he has an enormous amount of staying power in the game. Going back to my daughter's comment of no matter what everyone else says, his convictions and belief, he will actually stick by them and actually get through the hardest times.
turns.zh:
有一件事我们总会反复探讨，那就是在我们要涉足的领域，我们是否有进入市场的许可？每家公司都必须确保其提供的切入点和逻辑入口方式，往往取决于是否获得了在该市场竞争的许可？你是否有通往市场的路径来推广产品？仅仅开发出某个领域的出色产品，并不意味着就能实现大规模推广。因此，我们总会自问："我们正在打造的新品类或新功能，是否符合Box自主开发而非其他公司合作开发的逻辑？是符合思科自主开发而非其他公司合作开发的逻辑？"（00:31:18）  
这就是"许可竞争权"与"胜算权"的概念。只有获得了许可，我们才有在该领域胜出的权利；只有具备了通往市场的路径，我们才能将产品推向大众市场。若能把这些环节做好，投入研发的资金就能获得超额回报。反之，投入巨资却可能导致产品滞销。产品团队会抱怨："这些销售人员根本不明白。他们不知道怎么销售，尤其是企业软件领域。"而销售团队则反驳："这些产品经理根本不明白。他们不知道怎么开发产品。" （00:31:56）  
要避免这种争执，我们必须利用自身的规模优势，选择那些能让市场自然接受思科进入的领域。比如，当我们提议将GPU网络化并确保AI系统的可信性时，这对业界而言并非天方夜谭——毕竟过去40年我们在非AI领域的其他基础设施建设上积累了深厚经验。  
（00:32:35）  
这正是亚伦和我反复探讨的核心领域。顺便说一句，我很感激他能把这些观点从我脑中提炼出来。  
我从他身上学到的最重要一课是：永不言弃。坚持胜过智慧，耐力胜过智商——这句话在任何时候都适用。他固然极其聪明，但成功的关键在于他在赛道上展现出的持久韧性。  
回到我女儿的评论：无论别人怎么说，只要他坚信正确，就会坚持到底，挺过最艰难的时刻。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I totally believe that. I feel like I'm not the smartest person in the room usually, and I succeed in large part because I just work really hard.
turns.zh: 我完全认同这一点。我觉得自己通常不是房间里最聪明的人，但成功很大程度上源于我愿意付出极大的努力。

turns.speaker: Jeetu Patel
turns.en: You're pretty smart though. I've been watching your podcast for a while. You've done a pretty amazing job.
turns.zh: 不过你确实很聪明。我关注你的播客有一阵子了。你做得非常出色。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I appreciate it. In this permission to win concept, the reason I think it's so important is it's so easy to build stuff now. Everyone's just building, building, building, launching, launching, launching. It feels like this is an increasingly important lever is why will we win in this space? I'm curious if there's an example you can share either from Box or Cisco where it's just like, "Okay, this is like we're going to do this because we have the permission to play here."
turns.zh: 非常感谢。在这种“获准竞争”的理念中，我认为最重要的原因在于如今构建产品变得异常简单。每个人都在不停地建造、发布、推广。感觉这是一个越来越重要的杠杆——为什么我们能在这个领域胜出？我很好奇，你能否分享一下Box或思科的例子，说明他们是如何凭借“获准竞争”的理念，在某个领域占据先机的。

turns.speaker: Jeetu Patel
turns.en: I agree with you in the sense that if generating code is something that becomes abundant, that doesn't mean you're going to have better technology just because you can generate a lot of code. You still need human judgment, you still need a level of intuition on what problems are the right ones to solve. And yes, AI can help you with all of that, but it's not something that ... That's where humans have a superpower, they have instinct, and they can actually make sure that they can fulfill out a vision that says, "This is what I think this could be in the fullness of time." And so, that I think is pretty important. So, the easier it gets for us to get the bottlenecks out to generate code, the harder it gets for us to make sure that there's not AI slop in the market and that we actually are very selective on what are the things that are going to be the most important things that solve the most important problems moving forward? (00:35:01): Example of permission to play is, I mean, there's so many ideas that a company the size of Cisco, we have constantly new ideas that keep coming up. And then in those new ideas that keep coming up, people will always say, "Oh my goodness, this company is doing so well. We should just go into that market, or we should just go into this market." And 90% of the times, 99% of the times, I find myself saying no. And the reason for that is you have to be extremely selective of where you expend your calories. And that caloric expenditure is where if you expend your calories in a very focused way, the results you'll get from that focus area tend to be outsized and disproportionate. If you dissipate that caloric burn across multitude of different areas, nothing gets enough girth to be able to go out and drive it all the way through. And so, why are we not in business-to-consumer tech at Cisco? (00:36:10): Why are we not going out and building things that are very very B2C? Because I don't think we have a distribution channel that actually is within our DNA. I don't think that we've got permission to play there. That's an area where it would be extremely hard for people to growth that Cisco should be the one who's participating in that. Now can we do it? Of course we can do it. Is that where we want to go or do we want to go where there's so much opportunity in the areas where we can actually prosecute with the ability to operate from a position of strength that you'll just get a much better return for the dollar that you invest.
turns.zh: 我同意你的观点，即便生成代码变得司空见惯，但仅凭能生成大量代码并不意味着就能拥有更先进的技术。仍然需要人类的判断力，仍然需要对哪些问题值得解决的直觉。虽然AI可以在这方面提供帮助，但……这正是人类的超强能力所在——他们拥有本能，能够确保实现愿景，比如“这就是我认为未来可能实现的目标”。所以我认为这一点至关重要。生成代码的门槛降低了，但要确保市场上没有充斥着AI低质产品，并在未来真正专注于解决最重要的问题，这变得愈发困难。（00:35:01）：获准竞争的例子有很多。像思科这样的大型公司，总有源源不断的新想法涌现。在这些新想法中，人们总是会说：“天哪，这家公司发展得太好了。我们应该进军那个市场，或者那个市场。”但90%的情况下，99%的时候，我都会拒绝。因为你必须极其谨慎地选择投入精力的领域。若能高度聚焦于某个领域，成果往往会超出预期；但如果精力分散到多个不同领域，就没有任何项目能形成足够的规模并最终落地。所以为什么思科不涉足消费者科技领域？（00:36:10）：为什么我们不开发面向消费者的B2C产品？因为我认为我们的DNA里没有这样的分销渠道，也没有获准竞争的许可证。在这种领域，思科要想实现增长会极其困难。现在我们能做到吗？当然可以。但这是我们想要走的路吗？还是说我们应该专注于那些我们能够从强势地位出发、投入产出比更高的领域？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You mentioned Aaron as a CEO that you learned a lot from. I'm curious what other CEOs you've learned a lot from and what's something you learned from them?
turns.zh: 你提到Aaron是一位你从中收获颇丰的CEO。我很好奇还有哪些CEO能让你学到很多东西，以及你从他们身上学到了什么？

turns.speaker: Jeetu Patel
turns.en: Chuck Robbins is one of my favorite humans. And not just because I work for him, I work for him because he's one of my favorite humans. And what I've learned from him, he had this kind of great line. There was this piece of press that our media is very sensationalist by definition. They will try to create a very polarized view about the world where there actually isn't one. And most things in my life, things are not as extreme as you hear of the headlines of the media. It's somewhere in the middle. And there was one time that there was this article that ran, and it was about giving me an unnecessary amount of credit, and frankly, not giving Chuck as much credit about something that he has actually done. A lot of the movements that we've had internally wouldn't have happened if he had not hired me and given me agency to go do the things that I needed to get done. And he was very much completely in sync with me on what needed to happen. (00:38:13): And so, when I saw this article, I had no idea who the report, I reached out, I'm like, "Hey, I just want to let you know, this was not me saying it's someone." And she said, "Don't worry about it, man." What I've learned in life is, if you don't care about who gets the credit, you just go a lot farther in life." And it's so profound in so many ways that he's just way too confident to let anything. And so, the thing I've learned from Chuck is the importance of confidence and the importance of knowing what you're good at and where you're not good at. And where you're not good, you're going to assemble a team of people around you. He's just masterful at that, and it happens-
turns.zh: 查克·罗宾斯是我最欣赏的人之一。这不仅因为我为他工作，更是因为他本身就是我最崇拜的人。从他身上我学到的一点是，他曾说过一句至理名言。媒体本质上就是追求轰动效应的，他们总想把世界描绘成非黑即白的极端样态，而现实往往并非如此。我生活中的大多数事务，远比媒体头条所渲染的要平和得多。曾有篇报道将功劳过多地归于我，却对查克实际付出的努力着墨甚少。要知道，若不是他慧眼相中，授予我自主权去完成那些关键任务，我们内部推行的诸多改革根本无法落地。（00:38:13）当我看到那篇报道时，完全不知道是谁编造的。我联系了记者，解释道："嘿，我只想告诉你，这不是我说的，是别人造谣的。"她回道："别太在意，兄弟。" 这让我领悟到：若不执着于功劳归属，人生会走得更远。查克的自信堪称极致，他从不计较功劳归属，这份坦然令人钦佩。从他身上，我深深体会到自信的重要性——要清楚自己的专长所在，坦然承认不足之处，并组建一支优秀的团队协作。这种高超的领导艺术令人惊叹——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And by the way, he's the CEO of Cisco, in case people-
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，他可是思科的首席执行官，免得有人不知道——

turns.speaker: Jeetu Patel
turns.en: That's right. He's the CEO of Cisco. He is the chair of the business round table. He's very dear friend of mine. And I feel like there's a lot to learn from that kind of mental model and mindset. And I've been lucky enough, Lenny, that, and this is just dumb luck. The people that I've worked with and for are all very, very close to me, and I just don't let them go from my life. And so, one of the things, for example, is I worked with Aaron and then when I was leaving, it was very emotional, but I wanted to do something different. But we committed to each other that we are going to have dinner every six weeks. And Aaron, and there's another co-founder, Jeff Kweiser, and I, three of us. Every six weeks in Palo Alto we have dinner. And it's one of the most special things that I still do, and it's a tradition now, it's been going on for six years, and I love it. (00:40:02): You look at someone like Chuck, I start with my day with talking to him in the morning, we text each other. And then I end the day talking to them in the evening. And we probably touch base at least four or five times a day. They're not long conversations at all points in time, but we're constantly in contact with each other. And I feel like that only happens when you've established enough trust. My first post when I moved to California is this guy named Rick Devenuti and then another guy named Jeremy Burton. Rick Devenuti is still my coach. I see him every two weeks. Jeremy is someone that's a very dear friend of mine, and we're neighbors and be moved and bought a place next to his just so that we could be close to him. And these are special people in your life that have enriched your life in very different ways that I think you just have to make sure that you treasure.
turns.zh: 没错。他是思科的首席执行官。他是商业圆桌会议的主席。他是我非常要好的朋友。我觉得从他那种思维模式和心态中能学到很多东西。莱尼，我很幸运——这完全是运气使然。我共事和为之工作的人都与我关系非常亲密，我从不让他们从我的生活中消失。比如，我曾与亚伦共事，当我离开时，那真是一次感人的告别，但我想尝试些新东西。我们承诺每六周聚餐一次。亚伦、另一位联合创始人杰夫·奎泽尔和我三个人，在帕洛阿尔托每六周聚餐一次。这是我至今仍在坚持的最特别的传统，已坚持六年，我很喜欢这样做。（00:40:02）：说到查克这样的人，我每天从和他早晨的对话开始，一天结束时再和他聊聊。我们一天至少会四五次联系。虽然每次交流时间不长，但我们始终保持着联系。我觉得这种情谊只有在建立了足够信任的基础上才会产生。我搬到加州后的第一份工作是与里克·德文图蒂和杰里米·伯顿合作。里克至今仍是我的教练，我每两周见他一次。杰里米是我非常亲密的朋友，我们是邻居，搬家时特意选在他家附近，只为能离他更近。这些人丰富了你的生活，他们以各自独特的方式为你注入能量，你一定要珍惜这些珍贵的友情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Today's episode is brought to you by Samsara. If you listen to this podcast, you know that we spend a lot of time talking about building things that sit on a screen, onboarding funnels, mobile apps and checkout flows. Samsara is building products for the physical world, first responders racing to emergencies, truck drivers carrying critical supplies, construction workers building our cities and data centers. These are people who put everything on the line every single day, and Samsara's technology protects them. Samsara is solving complex problems at the intersection of hardware, software, and Edge AI, and their AI doesn't just detect events, it reasons about the intent and answers questions like, "Did that truck driver break abruptly because they were distracted, or was that a heroic act?" (00:41:38): If you want to ground LLMs in messy real-world telemetry or solve Edge AI constraints at a planetary scale, Samsara wants to talk to you. If you like playing with enormous datasets, moving fast and working in small teams, come help build the technology that makes the physical world safer and more efficient. Visit samsara.com/lenny to learn more. That's S-A-M-S-A-R-A.com/Lenny. So, you're currently CPO at Cisco. I think the team under you, IS it 25,000 people? Is that the right number?
turns.zh: 本期节目由Samsara赞助。如果你听过这个播客，就会知道我们经常讨论如何打造面向屏幕的应用、引导用户入门的流程、移动应用和结账流程。Samsara则致力于为现实世界打造产品，服务于紧急救援人员、运输关键物资的卡车司机、建设城市和数据中心的建筑工人。这些人每天都冒着生命危险，Samsara的技术为他们保驾护航。Samsara正在硬件、软件和边缘人工智能的交叉领域解决复杂问题，他们的人工智能不仅能检测事件，还能推理意图，回答诸如“卡车司机突然刹车是因为分心，还是因为英勇救人？”之类的问题。（00:41:38）：如果你想让大语言模型扎根于混乱的现实世界遥测数据，或是在全球范围内解决边缘人工智能的难题，Samsara期待与你交流。如果你喜欢处理海量数据、追求快速迭代并乐于在小团队中工作，就来帮助我们打造让现实世界更安全高效的技术吧。访问samsara.com/lenny了解更多信息。就是S-A-M-S-A-R-A.com/Lenny。

turns.speaker: Jeetu Patel
turns.en: We have about 30,000, but-
turns.zh: 我们大约有3万人，但——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: 30,000 people. Okay.
turns.zh: 3万人。好的。

turns.speaker: Jeetu Patel
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's something that you wish you'd known before taking on this role?
turns.zh: 在担任这个角色之前，你希望自己早点知道些什么？

turns.speaker: Jeetu Patel
turns.en: I don't know if it was ... I mean, I instinctively kind of knew it, but it was very, very accentuated at Cisco, because when people say, "Oh, is scale hard?" And my perspective has always been that the absence of scale is way harder than scale. What do I mean by that? If I have a startup with three people and we need to prosecute another idea, and that idea requires five people working on it, I have to go raise money, or I have to pivot my entire business. If you have 30,000 people and you have an idea that requires five people, you just figure out a way that you allocate the dollars internally and say, "Let's go prosecute this idea." So, in my mind, I always felt like absence of scale was way harder than the presence of scale. And operating within scale seemed like it was like, yeah, you have more opportunity to do it. (00:43:23): What I found over the years, not just at Cisco, but even when I ... Because I ran a small startup in Chicago for 17 years before I moved over to the Valley, what I found in the large companies is, the communication framework and the lossiness of communication, the telephone game, so to say, has a profoundly negative effect if you're not intentional about it and if you're not careful of it. And there was this board member that we had, there's a couple board members, our lead director, Michael Capellas is amazing. There's this other board member, Kevin is amazing, and then there's this one board member, Wes Bush, who we recently rolled off, but he used to be on our board. (00:44:09): And when I got this job, he pulled me aside, said, "Jeetu, I'm going to tell you something. I'm going to give you some advice, and take it or leave it, but I think it's going to be important for you to keep it in mind." I'm like, "What's that?" And he goes, "Whatever you do, don't think about your story of the company as a marketing exercise. Think about it as the most intrinsic foundational exercise of the company. And always be the custodian of the message. Don't delegate that to someone else to give. Because if you have 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 layers between you and the person who's actually doing the job in the front line, what you don't want to do is play the telephone game and assume that people will just cascade it when you go to your team and then say, 'Okay, that team will cascade to the next team, cascade to the next team, cascade to the next team.' Every one of them will add a flavor with well-intentioned, and then by the time it gets to the end, people won't know what it is. So always own telling the story." (00:45:14): And I'm like, "That seems like it's a lot because we have a very broad portfolio. We do all of these events. It's like, I'm going to have to stand on stage for 90 minutes and just talk about it." He's like, "Please do that. Make sure you don't." (00:45:27): And initially, the hidden benefit that came out of it that I did not realize is it massively, Lenny, simplified our business. And you know why? Because we have such a broad business with so many different industries, it's impossible for someone to be a deep expert in every single one of them across the board. There's just way too much surface area. But the things that we want to convey to the market that the market should take away from us, if that story is not something that I understand well enough to be able to convey it, how do I first expect 20,000 of my sellers to be able to go tell it to the market? And how do I expect my customers to be able to digest that story? There's zero chance that would happen. (00:46:16): And so, that was my big takeaway from this, which is don't delegate the storytelling. And the storytelling is not a marketing exercise after you built the product. The story is why you build the product to make the story come real. And so, make sure that the story is there first, and then that story has evidence and proof based on the products that you're building.
turns.zh:
我不知道是不是……我是说，我本能地意识到这一点，但在思科公司，这种情况尤为明显。当人们问“哦，扩大规模很难吗？”时，我的观点始终是，缺乏规模比追求规模要难得多。我这么说是什么意思呢？如果我有一家只有三人的初创公司，需要推进另一个创意，而这个创意需要五人团队合作，我就得去融资，或者彻底转型整个业务。但如果你有3万名员工，有个想法只需要五人团队，你只需在内部重新分配资源，然后说：“让我们去推进这个创意。”所以在我看来，缺乏规模比拥有规模要难得多。在规模化运营的环境中，似乎确实有更多机会去实现目标。（00:43:23）：多年来，我发现不只是在思科，甚至在我搬到硅谷之前在芝加哥经营17年的小型初创公司时，在大公司里，沟通框架和沟通效率低下——可以说类似“传话游戏”——如果不刻意去改善，带来的负面影响非常严重。我们曾有一位董事会成员，米切尔·卡佩拉斯（Michael Capellas）非常出色，还有凯文（Kevin）也很棒，但最近离职的韦斯·布什（Wes Bush）之前也在董事会。（00:44:09）：我刚接手这份工作时，他把我拉到一边说：“杰图，我要告诉你一件事。我给你些建议，听不听随你，但我觉得你得谨记在心。”我问：“什么事？”他说：“无论如何，都别把公司的故事当作营销手段。要把它视为公司最核心的基础建设。永远做信息传递的把关人。别把这项任务委托给别人。因为如果你和一线团队之间隔着三、四、五、六、七层管理层，你不想玩传话游戏，然后指望下属逐级传达，最后人们都理解不了原意。所以故事的讲述必须由你亲自完成。”（00:45:14）：我说：“这听起来责任重大，因为我们业务范围很广，活动也很多。我得站在台上讲90分钟。”他说：“请务必这么做。别推辞。”（00:45:27）：最初，我没有意识到这背后隐藏着巨大的好处——它极大地简化了我们的业务。为什么呢？因为我们的业务范围广泛，涉及众多不同行业，要让每个员工都成为全能专家是不现实的。面太广了。但如果我们想传达给市场的东西，市场应该能准确理解。如果我连自己都理解不透彻，又怎么能指望2万名销售人员去向市场传达呢？又怎么能指望客户消化这些信息呢？那根本不可能。（00:46:16）：所以，这就是我最大的收获。
也就是说，不要把讲故事的任务交给别人。讲故事不应是在产品研发完成后才进行的营销活动。而是讲故事的初衷，正是推动你去开发这款产品的动力。因此，首先要确保故事本身存在，然后再用你正在开发的产品为这个故事提供证据和佐证。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I had a conversation with Matt MacInnis, who's COO now CPO at Rippling, and hit a similar piece of advice, which I think is also, it's like adjacent advice, which is "The intensity of an idea or a plan drops at every level that it goes from CO to the next layer and layer. And your job as a leader is to maintain that intensity, not to buffer it from the employees, but to maintain exactly the same intensity."" And it feels like that's in addition to also just keep the story the same. Like don't filter it, don't change it. Although your advice is even different, just like you actually go to the team working on it and tell the story yourself. Don't even let-
turns.zh:
我与Rippling公司的首席运营官（现任首席产品官）马特·麦金尼斯（Matt MacInnis）进行了交流，听到了一个类似的建议——我认为这两者其实有相通之处，那就是：“一个想法或计划的强度在从CO（首席运营官）层级到下层级传递的过程中会逐渐减弱。作为领导者，你的职责是保持这种强度，而不是将其隔绝于员工，而是要确保强度始终如一。” 

这似乎不仅仅意味着要保持故事的连贯性，还意味着不进行过滤或改动。即便你的建议有所不同，也要亲自到团队中去讲述这个故事，绝不能让——

turns.speaker: Jeetu Patel
turns.en: I want to make sure that they hear it from me directly so that there's no lossiness. We have this concept in networking called packet loss. When you actually send packets over a wire and you have a loss of packet, then actually there's loss of data. You don't want to have packet loss in your storytelling from you to the person on the front line because-
turns.zh: 我要确保他们直接从我这里听到，这样才能避免信息失真。网络领域有个术语叫“数据包丢失”。当数据包通过网线传输时，如果有数据包丢失，实际上就是数据的损失。在你向一线员工传达故事时，同样不能出现信息丢失，因为——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The direct ethernet Cat 5 connection.
turns.zh: 这就像直接的以太网Cat 5连接。

turns.speaker: Jeetu Patel
turns.en: This is just a direct connection and there's no packet loss of this one. You got to make sure it gets to the intended audience. And I think the reason for that is, as companies get large, they can lose touch with the front lines. Everyone gets really good with the math of the business, but they don't really always preserve the soul of the business. And there's a lossiness that happens, because if you have seven, eight layers between you and the front line, even the message that's coming back to you from them is actually getting lossy. (00:48:15): And so what you have to do is just preserve ... And I think what was said earlier about the intensity is the same way, which is you got to preserve the intensity. You got to preserve the sanctity of the message, and you got to preserve the clarity of the message so that everyone is clear on the direction we're going down. And if you can stay clear and stay motivated about that direction and make sure that everyone's on the same page and what needs to be done to execute, you will have success. If not, you'll actually have guaranteed failure.
turns.zh: 这就是直接的连接，没有数据包丢失的问题。你必须确保信息准确传达给目标受众。我认为原因在于，随着公司规模扩大，他们可能会与一线员工失去联系。每个人都精通商业运算，但却未必能守护住企业的灵魂。这就会导致信息失真，因为如果你和一线员工之间隔着七八层管理层，传回给你的信息也会逐渐失真。（00:48:15）所以你必须保持……我认为前面提到的保持强度同样重要，即你要保持信息的完整性，确保传达的信息准确无误，让每个人都清楚我们的发展方向。如果你能保持清晰的方向，保持动力，确保所有人同心协力完成任务，你就能取得成功。反之，则注定失败。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How do you actually operationalize this without just being overloaded with work and constantly having to meet with every team and remind them of the story?
turns.zh: 那如何在不被工作压得喘不过气、不必频繁与每个团队开会提醒他们故事要点的前提下，将这一理念落到实处呢？

turns.speaker: Jeetu Patel
turns.en: The first thing I feel is, you have to have very clear thinking because the clarity of thought is what brings clarity of communication. So, you have to spend the time with your team in sweating the details on what it is that you want to do and why you want to do it. The context of why is so lost, and constantly reminding people why it's important and having the least amount of asymmetry between the topmost layer in the organization and the bottommost layer is super. Now, by the way, I'm a Section 16 officer. There are certain things that, for example, you're in a quiet period you can't go talk about to someone else during that time period, but that's not allowed. However, the most amount of context that you can provide them in the way that you can because you're allowed to, the better off you are. (00:49:47): And always treat people like adults. What I've found is, oftentimes when you go into corporate environments, like people start becoming very sterile in the facts that they provide. And sometimes it's okay to just say, "Hey, we screwed up here. This was really bad." That's not meant to ... One of the things that I found to be very counterintuitive, because every management book that you read will tell you otherwise. What do they say? Praise in public and criticize in private. I fundamentally disagree with that notion. I think what you have to do is establish enough trust among the team so that you are comfortable critiquing and debating in public. But when you're in private, take that moment to build the trust. Because if you build that trust and you tell them that you've got their back and you create a level of safety there in public, you don't want to be in a mode of posturing. (00:50:57): You want to be in a mode of problem-solving. When you're just giving people perfunctory compliments all the time, and everything's just hunky-dory. Rose-colored glass is great. All your dashboards look green, but you're growing the business at 1.5%. There's an asymmetry there, something's broken. It's like, what do we need to do over here? And so what I tend to do is use the exact opposite approach. I tend to be very, very direct in public, be respectful, but be direct in public. This is not working. Let me tell you why it's not working. We got to face the facts. And then be very, very clear with people that you got their back in private. And don't be stingy with words on that front, because I feel like there are times when people are very stingy with words with people in private. You can't be stingy with words over there. (00:51:52): And don't be stingy with critique in public, because I think people need to make sure that, "We are solving problems together." And if we don't know the play that we're executing, if we don't know the things that we're going to need to do, then I am not really certain. If you're making collective progress, and I think it's not going to be fulfilling to either you or the recipient at some point, and those compliments will feel hollow because you didn't mean them. Because you were trying to put it in between. Like Ben Horowitz says, and hard things about hard things that you have a shit sandwich. You say something really nice to someone, then you say something that's not really nice, and then you put no, just treat people like adults. Tell them the facts, watch your tone. I still have to work on that. There are times when I get very passionate. People think like, but watch your tone and make sure that you debate. Conflict is a necessary condition of business, but the only way that you can have productive conflict is if you've established trust. (00:52:54): And the only way that you can establish trust is by making sure that you spend the time to establish the trust. So spend the time to establish the trust, but then focus on the best idea, winning and actually having the debate.
turns.zh:
首先，我觉得你必须保持清晰的思维，因为思维的清晰度决定了沟通的清晰度。因此，你需要花时间与团队一起仔细思考你想做什么以及为什么要做这件事。人们往往忽视了"为什么"的背景，持续提醒大家事情的重要性，并尽可能减少组织高层与基层之间的信息不对称，这非常重要。  

（00:49:47）另外，要始终把人们当作成年人来对待。我发现，在企业环境中，人们提供的信息往往过于刻板。有时坦率地说：“嘿，我们在这里搞砸了。这真的很糟糕。”并没有什么问题。（00:50:57）但我发现最违背直觉的一点是，所有管理书籍都教导你要公开表扬、私下批评。我对此完全不同意。我认为你必须在团队中建立足够的信任，让大家在公开场合能够自由地批评和讨论。但在私下交流时，要抓住机会巩固信任。如果你建立了这种信任，公开场合告诉他们你会支持他们，并营造安全感，就不必故作姿态，而是要专注于解决问题。当你总是敷衍地夸奖别人，一切看似美好时，那就是在蒙蔽众人。你的仪表盘上数字全绿，但业务增长只有1.5%。这里存在不对称问题，问题出在哪里？所以我的做法恰恰相反。我在公开场合非常直接，但保持尊重；在私下也要明确告诉他们你会支持他们。别吝啬于表达，因为私下里人们往往很吝啬。（00:51:52）同样，在公开场合批评时也要直言不讳，因为人们需要确信“我们正在共同解决问题”。如果我们不清楚执行的策略，不知道需要做什么，那我就没把握了。如果你在共同进步，但最终让双方都无法获得满足，那这些赞美就会显得空洞，因为你并非真心实意，而是夹带私货。正如本·霍洛维茨所说，面对难题时，你可能会陷入"吃了屎三明治"的困境——先说些好听的，再说些难听的，最后又故作轻松。（00:52:17）所以要始终把人们当作成年人来对待。告诉他们事实，注意语气。这一点我还需要努力改进，有时我会过于激动。人们会觉得"但要注意语气"，确保辩论的正向。冲突是商业的必要条件，但只有通过建设性的冲突才能达成共赢。
就好比你已经建立了信任关系。（00:52:54）：而建立信任的唯一方法，就是确保你花时间去建立这种信任。因此，先花时间建立信任，但之后要专注于最优方案、争取胜利，并切实开展辩论。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there maybe one more lesson that you've learned from this? Or I guess it's something you wish you'd known before getting into this role? Is there anything else that comes to mind?
turns.zh: 或许你还能从中吸取其他教训？或者你希望在接手这个角色之前就了解这些情况？还有什么其他想法吗？

turns.speaker: Jeetu Patel
turns.en: I was an apps guy. I operated in the apps layer. I worked at Box. And even when I was at EMC, I was building apps that you built for the end user. Infrastructure is a different game. And the thing that I learned about infrastructure is, you don't always get the glory, but you always get the blame.
turns.zh: 我曾是一名专注于应用层开发的工程师。我在Box工作过，即便在EMC任职时，我也主要负责为终端用户开发应用程序。但基础设施领域完全不同。关于基础设施，我领悟到的一点是，你可能不会因此获得赞誉，但却总是要承担责任。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Perfect.
turns.zh: 太对了。

turns.speaker: Jeetu Patel
turns.en: And you have to be comfortable with the fact that you are working in a way that other people get the glory. Great infrastructure companies, the application companies get the glory when they're running on that infrastructure. So, you have to be hardwired in infrastructure to orient on your ecosystem success, not just your own success. And that is probably one of the lessons that I learned at Cisco in a very stark way, which I didn't fully appreciate it until I got into the details of the infrastructure going, "Wow, if this thing doesn't work," we were ... Every single time, our infrastructure doesn't work. This morning I was with a medical institution, I was with a healthcare company this morning, and they were telling me they were very complimentary. They were thanking us on the partnership. I asked them, "Why are you doubling down with us?" And they're like, "Because when the infrastructure doesn't work, people die. Someone doesn't get dialysis, someone doesn't get a surgery done, and we need to make sure that we're working with someone with the infrastructure is working." (00:55:02): And so, I feel like at that point in time, you can't be navel-gazing too much about, "Look how cool you are, because you did something." You have to just make sure that you're really immediately shifting your focus to, what does the customer do and what does the ecosystem do with your infrastructure so that the outcome is achieved? And you have to get very outcome oriented. And I feel like that was something that I always intellectually knew, but I didn't fully realize it until I came here on how important of a mindset shift that is. You are not talking about yourself, you're talking about the system just working. No one will come and tell you, "Hey, Jeetu, thank you so much. My network worked today." But the moment it doesn't work, they're going to call you and say, "You know what? My network's not working, and my people can't work and patients are dying in the hospital." I think you just have to be comfortable with that.
turns.zh: 你必须坦然接受，自己所做的工作会让别人获得荣誉。优秀的基础设施公司，当应用程序在其基础设施上运行时，应用程序公司会赢得赞誉。因此，在基础设施领域，你必须以生态系统成功为导向，而非仅仅关注自身的成功。这或许是我在思科最深刻的领悟，直到深入了解基础设施运作细节后，我才充分意识到这一点——"哇，如果基础设施出了问题，后果不堪设想。"（00:55:02）比如，今天我与一家医疗机构会面，合作方对我们的合作赞誉有加。他们感谢我们的合作伙伴关系时，我问道："为何你们要与我们深化合作？"对方回答："因为基础设施一旦出问题，人们就会丧命。有人得不到透析治疗，有人无法接受手术，我们必须确保与能保障基础设施正常运转的合作伙伴合作。" 所以，在那种时刻，你不能过于自我陶醉，感叹"我们太棒了"，而是要立即将注意力转向客户如何使用基础设施，以及生态系统如何依托你的基础设施实现目标。你必须以结果为导向。我觉得自己对此心知肚明，但直到来到这里，我才深刻体会到这种思维转变的重要性。你谈论的不是自己，而是整个系统能否正常运转。没人会主动说"嘿，吉图，今天我的网络运行得很棒。"但一旦出现故障，他们就会打电话抱怨："你们的网络又出问题了，我的团队无法工作了，医院里的患者命悬一线。" 我觉得你必须坦然接受这种现实。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's so interesting how this lesson connects so directly to the lesson you learned from Chuck, the CEO of Cisco, which is, "Don't expect the praise and the credit. You need to be comfortable with other people getting credit for your work."
turns.zh: 有趣的是，这一教训与你从思科首席执行官查克那里学到的经验高度契合——"别指望赞誉和功劳。要习惯别人因你的工作而获得荣誉。"

turns.speaker: Jeetu Patel
turns.en: That's right. By the way, it's not surprising given that he spent, I don't know, 26, 28 years over here, you know why that he's conditioned with the fact that he's focused on other people succeeding from it. From your work.
turns.zh: 没错。顺便说一句，这并不令人意外，毕竟他在这里工作了26、28年，难怪他会形成这样的思维模式——关注他人而非自己。关注你的工作成果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It feels like there's so many metaphors corollaries to networking as a way to think about leadership and living life.
turns.zh: 似乎有很多隐喻和推论，都能以网络为切入点，来思考领导力和生活方式。

turns.speaker: Jeetu Patel
turns.en: It really is.
turns.zh: 确实如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh man, I bet you guys have all kinds of examples.
turns.zh: 天哪，我敢打赌你们肯定能举出各种各样的例子。

turns.speaker: Jeetu Patel
turns.en: It's a good exercise to actually go through and create the corollary of parallelism between life and networks.
turns.zh: 实际上，去梳理并总结生活与网络之间的平行关系是个不错的练习。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm thinking about just how many friends, like Dunbar's number, how many notes can you have in a network before it starts to slow down? Maybe 150. Oh, man. Okay. Anyway, I like that your mind's spinning.
turns.zh: 我在思考像邓巴数这样的概念——在一个社交网络中，当好友数量超过某个临界值时，系统会开始变得迟缓。或许150人左右？天哪。好吧，不管怎样，我很欣赏你思维的活跃度。

turns.speaker: Jeetu Patel
turns.en: I'm thinking how many can you have? I think more than 150, for sure.
turns.zh: 我在想这个临界值到底是多少？我觉得肯定超过150人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I also was thinking about Intel. The whole Intel Inside move was such a clever way to break through that where no one would know Intel and so they're just like, slap a sticker of Intel Inside.
turns.zh: 我还想到了英特尔。“Intel Inside”这个营销策略真是天才之作——他们巧妙地避开了让用户直接联想到英特尔品牌的风险，直接贴上“Intel Inside”的标签。

turns.speaker: Jeetu Patel
turns.en: And by the way, they are. Lipu is a very dear friend. Pat Gelsinger used to be my mentor at EMC. And so both those people that have had such a profound contribution to that industry in general. When you start thinking about them, they're very, very much on that mode.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，他们确实是。李普是位非常亲密的朋友。帕特·吉尔辛格曾是我在EMC时的导师。这两人都为整个行业做出了深远贡献。当你回想起他们时，他们无疑都是业界的传奇人物。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I could see how you pull together this insane collection of humans, just feels like you're just friends with everybody.
turns.zh: 我能想象你如何汇聚这群令人惊叹的人脉，感觉你简直和所有人都熟识。

turns.speaker: Jeetu Patel
turns.en: I feel like it's, life's too short not to be, and I'm only friends with people that I feel are good human beings. What I try not to do is I try to minimize my time no matter how successful they are with people whose energy I don't vibe with, because I think life's too short. And in my mind, one of the most off-putting things is, look, all of us have a healthy ego. There are times when ego gets manifested with insecurity and you have to make sure that you're at least self-aware enough to know when your ego is starting to take over your behavior in a way that's counterproductive. And all of those things are super important. But what I think is extremely important is that you ... Life is just fun to live when you love the people you are around. (00:58:43): Can I digress for a second in this one story that ... I'll tell you the story that was ... So my mother was, she passed away two and a half years ago, but she was extremely sick in the hospital for eight weeks before she passed away. And I was very close to my mom. She was my everything and we were only child. I grew up with a rough childhood. My dad was a high-stakes kind of conn man, like Bernie Madoff. I didn't want to be any part of that. So I had actually left India, come over here, hadn't seen him. And so he was very abusive to my mom. So there was a bunch of that that had happened. (00:59:27): And so, we had had a very difficult early childhood life for me, and her and I had bonded during that time at a very deep level. And so when she came to America, she always wanted to have her own place, but she lived very close by and she was very dependent on me emotionally in every way. And so, I had almost become a parent to her. (01:00:00): And at the last eight weeks things flipped and she became a parent again. And so we were getting to the point where she was ending her journey. And I was sitting one in the morning at the bedside by her in the hospital. I was living in the hospital at the time. And she was sleeping and I was just crying profusely. And she wakes up, and she knows why I'm crying, because she's going to be gone soon. And she looks at me, Lenny, and she's like all perplexed and she's like, "I had no idea that you loved me so much." Now, by the way, this is the most abnormal thing for me to hear, because I'm like, "What are you talking about mom? Like you're one of the most important people in my life." And everything that I did was to make sure that my mom was okay. Why did it feel that way to her? Because she didn't know how I was thinking. (01:01:10): And that kind of notion of people don't know what's going on in your mind is so important that my biggest lesson from that was, "Don't be stingy with words." Because even my mother that knows me inside and out didn't know how much I loved her, that there's no chance that people in the business world are going to know how you feel if you're not explicit with them. And so, I'm actually very clear with people, when I find them and when I find them rewarding, I let them know how much they mean, because I genuinely find a lot of energy coming out of that. And B, the circle of friends just keeps getting bigger and bigger and bigger. And I found that to be a super rewarding thing in life. And you're right, most of the people that were at the AI Summit are dear friends, and isn't that just a better way to live life?
turns.zh: 我觉得人生太短暂了，不值得把时间浪费在与那些不善良的人交往上。我尽量减少与那些精力不符的人相处的时间，无论他们多么成功，因为我觉得人生太短暂了。在我看来，最令人反感的事情之一是，所有人都有健康的自尊心。但有时自尊会因不安全感而显露出来，你必须确保自己至少能意识到，当自尊开始以适得其反的方式主导你的行为时，要及时调整。这些都非常重要。但我认为最重要的是，你……当你喜欢身边的人时，生活才会有趣。（00:58:43）：我能稍微讲讲这个故事吗……我来讲讲这个故事吧……我母亲两年半前去世了，但她在去世前在医院住了八周，病情非常严重。我和母亲关系极为亲密。她是我的一切，我们是独生子女。我童年过得很艰难。我的父亲是个高风险的骗子，像伯尼·麦道夫那样的人。我不想和他有任何瓜葛。所以我离开了印度，来到这里，从此再没见过他。他对母亲的虐待非常严重，种种恶行不胜枚举。（00:59:27）……所以，对我和她来说，童年生活非常艰难，那段时间我们建立了深厚的情感纽带。她来美国后，总想有自己的住处，但住得离我很近，在各方面都非常依赖我。于是我几乎成了她的家长。（01:00:00）……但最后八周情况急转直下，她又成了我的家长。到了她生命即将结束的时候，我凌晨一点坐在医院病床边。她当时住院，我也住在医院。她睡着了，我哭得很伤心。她醒来后，知道我为什么哭，因为她快要离开了。她看着我，莱尼，一脸困惑地说：“我不知道你这么爱我。”说实话，这对我来说太不正常了，因为我说：“妈妈，你在说什么呀？你是我生命中最重要的人之一。”我所做的一切都是为了确保母亲安好。为什么她会这样觉得？因为她不知道我在想什么。（01:01:10）……人们不了解你的想法，这一点太重要了。我从中得到的最大教训是“别吝啬表达”。就连对我了如指掌的母亲都不知道我有多爱她，更别说商界的人了。所以我现在和人交流时非常坦诚。当我发现他们值得时，就会告诉他们他们对我有多重要，因为这真的能给我带来能量。其次，朋友圈子越来越大。我发现这真是生活最美好的部分。没错，参加AI峰会的大多数人都是好朋友，这难道不是更好的生活方式吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think we've uncovered one of the secrets of your success, which is just tell people how you feel and help them see that you appreciate them. Make it clear that you appreciate them, that you value them, which is a lot of people don't do, they just assume they know that they like you.
turns.zh: 我觉得我们已经揭示了你成功的秘诀之一，那就是告诉人们你的感受，帮助他们明白你欣赏他们。明确表达你对他们的赞赏和重视——这正是许多人做不到的，他们只是想当然地认为对方知道自己喜欢他们。

turns.speaker: Jeetu Patel
turns.en: And don't make it fake.
turns.zh: 别装模作样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And don't make it fake.
turns.zh: 别装模作样。

turns.speaker: Jeetu Patel
turns.en: Don't make it fake. If you don't love someone, don't tell them you love them. That's the other thing that I have.
turns.zh: 别装模作样。如果你不爱某个人，别告诉他们你爱他们。这也是我领悟到的另一件事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's so interesting. We just did a little interview kind of thing with my mother-in-law meant for our son, just for him to have when he's older. They just interviewed her about her story and stuff and they asked her at the end of it, "What's something you want Jude," which is his name, "to know, a lesson to learn from you?" And it's to just, if you love someone, tell them you love them as much as you can.
turns.zh: 太有趣了。我们刚刚为我岳母做了一个小采访，专门为我们的儿子准备的，等他长大后可以看看。他们采访了她的人生故事之类的，最后问她：“你希望朱德（Jude，指她孙子）知道什么，给你的人生启示？”她说就是，如果你爱某个人，尽可能多地告诉他们你爱他们。

turns.speaker: Jeetu Patel
turns.en: Yeah, that's so true. You're so intentional about the way in which you do these things. I wish I'd done a, I should do that now. Now I think about it, do a podcast for my daughter that's only for her when she gets older.
turns.zh: 是啊，这太对了。你做这些事时总是很有心。我真希望我也做过，现在就该行动了。现在回想起来，应该为我女儿做一个播客，等她长大了再听。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'll send you these. This group, they do this. I think they're in the Bay Area, but it's incredible. It's a whole documentary thing where they interview you, film your life for a little bit and then make a whole documentary.
turns.zh: 我会把这些发给你。这个团队做得很棒。他们在湾区，但真的很棒。他们会拍摄你的生活，制作一部完整的纪录片。

turns.speaker: Jeetu Patel
turns.en: Oh really? Oh, wow. I'd love that actually.
turns.zh: 哦，真的吗？哇，我其实很想体验一下。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yes. Oh, man. They're going to get a lot of business right now.
turns.zh: 是的。天哪。他们现在肯定生意火爆。

turns.speaker: Jeetu Patel
turns.en: There you go.
turns.zh: 就说到这吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me end with a question around just your journey. So today you lead product at a 90,000 person company. You manage 30,000 people. Like you said, you grew up in India in Bombay very far outside Silicon Valley. A lot of people hearing this today are kind of in a similar boat. They're way outside of the valley, maybe don't have a lot of obvious way to break in. They don't have a lot of opportunity and they see someone like you and that's their dream. What would your advice be to someone in that place right now?
turns.zh: 最后我想问问你的成长历程。如今你领导着一家拥有9万名员工的公司的产品团队，管理着3万名员工。正如你所说，你在印度孟买长大，那里离硅谷相隔万里。而如今许多听众也处于类似境遇——他们远离硅谷，似乎没有明显的切入途径，机会渺茫，看到像你这样的人，就燃起了梦想。对于此刻身处这种环境的人，你有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Jeetu Patel
turns.en: The platform that you choose and the quality of problems that you pick to solve actually determine a lot of the path of success for you. And typically harder problems have a higher likelihood of success. Because the harder problems are the ones that attract better people to that problem and business as a team sport. And if you attract people to the problems that are hard and important enough to solve, then you get the best team, and you get the best team, your odds are winning just go up exponentially. So most people think I'm going to go out and pick an easy enough problem to solve. And it's like you don't get the best-team attracted to you to start up a lemonade stand, very important job. But that might not be the thing that actually gets the best team to come to you. But if you actually pick a hard enough problem to solve, you'll get the best team to come. (01:04:54): So that's one. Number two, I'd say that you can teach and learn a lot of things in life. I don't think you can learn hunger or you can't teach hunger. So find what you're intrinsically hungry about and make sure that you try to pursue that area. And that's different from passion about something. It's like in everything that you do in work, you have to just understand the formula that there's going to be 30% of the stuff that you do at work that you're just going to hate. And you have to get used to things that you hate that you have to do. But further, but find something that you're really hungry about that makes you want to come in to work every day, because the mission is worth the expenditure of energy that you're putting into it. (01:05:50): And I'll leave you with a story which was, I hadn't gone to India in a long time. When I left India, I didn't go back. I left in '91 and I hadn't gone back in any kind of meaningful way until 2017 because of all the trauma in childhood. For whatever reason, I hadn't gone back. But I took my daughter and we went to Augra to see the Taj Mahal and we went there and there was this tour guide, his name was Raj. And this tour guide was like he understood so much about the product that he was selling, which was the tour of the Taj Mahal. I don't know if he was making the shit up or not, but it sounded really good and he seemed like he was kind of early on it. (01:06:34): But when we were walking back, there's all these people and he would just start talking to them and he'd bust out in different languages. He'd talk to someone in German, talk to someone in French, someone in Spanish, someone in Hindi, someone in. And at some point in time in Mandarin. And at some point in time I stopped, "Dude, how many languages do you speak?" (01:06:51): He's like, "Oh, I speak, I don't know, 12 or 14 or some ridiculous number. But I try to learn a new language every year." I'm like, "Oh, why is that?" And he goes, "Well, I just want to honor the people that come here and not be presumptuous that they will speak in the language that I know." I want to speak in their language. And I'm thinking to myself, I was a box at the time. I'm like, "This guy is smarter than every person on the executive team and probably just as smart as every salesperson we have, but he's making $10 a day and all of us are enjoying this amazing life, and it's because we have access to a platform and he doesn't." So when people start confusing life thinking that, "Everything that I've earned is because of my amazing abilities." I always question that, because there's a lot of luck in this thing. (01:07:45): But when luck does present itself, be extremely prepared to capitalize on it. And make sure that you pick the platform that can actually give you that springboard. Because platforms really matter. And if we, like I had the platform and benefit of America, of education, of being in tech, of having great friends and mentors, all of those things created compounding value. But I intentionally sought out those platforms, seek out the platform, be obsessed about being extremely prepared, and don't be intellectually lazy. Laziness is not a good trait. So do the preparation that's needed. And then just make sure that during that time period that you're doing, if you build a community around you of people that are vested in your success, I think it's just, life is just a more fun way to live it, rather than being the lone wolf that's going at it by themselves. (01:08:54): And that's why I always feel like making sure that you are expressive and communicative and don't try to carry the entire world's burden on your shoulders, but actually share it with people with you, the people that you share it with actually appreciate that you're sharing it with them. (01:09:13): And most people in the world love to help. So ask for the help, but make sure that that help is not transactional. And don't just go to them when you need something. Actually try to add value first for a long enough amount of time, not because at some point you might need something from them, just hard-wire yourself into adding value to others. And then eventually that value starts showing up, and life's just a better way to live life. And I do feel like right now it's hard for kids getting into the workforce and all of that. So, don't lose hope and stay persistent and have stamina, because these things go up and down. But if you kind of stick with it, the people that have the most amount of persistence, it's very seldom that they don't end up winning.
turns.zh:
您选择的平台以及您挑选的待解决问题的质量，实际上决定了您成功之路的很大一部分。通常来说，更难的问题成功的概率更高。因为更难的问题能吸引更优秀的人才参与其中，商业本质上是一项团队运动。如果您能吸引人们参与足够困难且重要的问题，那么您就能组建最优秀的团队，而拥有最优秀的团队，成功的概率就会呈指数级增长。所以大多数人会想，我要去找一个足够容易解决的问题。但如果你去摆柠檬水摊，就很难吸引到优秀的团队成员——这虽然是一份重要的工作，但未必能吸引到最优秀的团队。然而，如果您选择一个足够困难且重要的问题去解决，您就能吸引到最优秀的团队。（01:04:54）  

第二点，我想说人生中有很多东西是可以学习和领悟的。我认为你无法教会别人饥饿感，也无法教会别人不饥饿。所以要找到你内心真正渴望的东西，并确保努力去追寻那个领域。这和对某件事的热情不同。在工作中，你必须明白一个规律：工作中30%的事情你会讨厌，但你必须习惯这些讨厌的事。更重要的是，找到真正能让你每天乐在其中的工作，因为这份工作的使命值得你投入精力。（01:05:50）  

我最后想讲一个故事。我很久没去印度了。离开印度后，我再也没有真正回去过。1991年离开后，直到2017年我才以一种有意义的方式重返故土，因为童年留下了太多创伤。不知为何，我一直没有回去。但我带着女儿去阿格拉看泰姬陵，导游叫拉杰。他对泰姬陵之旅的讲解极其专业，不知是即兴发挥还是事先准备，反正听起来很棒，感觉他对这份工作很上心。（01:06:34）  

回程时，周围都是游客，他会用不同语言与他们交流。先是德语，接着法语、西班牙语、印地语，最后还用了中文。我忍不住问：“老兄，你会多少种语言？”  
他说：“哦，我不知道，大概12种、14种吧，反正每年都会学一门新语言。”  
我问：“为什么要这样做？”  
他回答：“我想尊重每位游客，不假定他们会说我的语言，而是用他们的语言交流。” 我当时很震惊，心想：“这家伙比高管团队里的任何人都聪明，可能和我们的每个销售员一样聪明，但他每天只赚10美元，而我们却过着优渥的生活，就因为我们有平台，而他没有。” 所以当人们开始把生活想得太简单，认为“我所取得的一切都是因为我的非凡能力”时，我总会质疑这种想法，因为成功中有很多运气的成分。（01:07:45）
充分利用这些机会。同时，要确保你选择的平台能够真正为你提供跳板。因为平台至关重要。就拿我自己来说，得益于美国的平台、教育资源、科技行业的机遇，以及优秀的朋友和导师的支持，这些因素共同创造了复合价值。但我有意识地寻找这些平台，主动争取机遇，始终保持极度充分的准备，绝不存在思维上的懒惰。懒惰绝非好品质。因此，做好必要的准备工作至关重要。另外，要确保在奋斗期间，围绕自己建立一群真心希望你成功的团队，这样生活会更加有趣，远胜过独自奋战的孤军奋战。（01:08:54）正因如此，我始终强调要保持开放沟通，别试图独自承担全世界的重担，而是要与他人分享你的负担。（01:09:13）世界上大多数人都乐于助人。所以主动寻求帮助，但要注意这种帮助不应是交易性的，别只在需要时才去找他们。先为他人创造价值，坚持足够长的时间——不是为了从他们那里获取回报，而是要养成为他人创造价值的习惯。最终，这些价值会反馈回来，生活也会因此更加美好。如今，年轻人进入职场面临诸多挑战，但请不要失去希望，保持坚韧和耐力，因为人生起起落落。只要坚持不懈，那些最具耐力的人最终必将赢得成功。
